title: Assurance: confidence for the governance board
blurb: Explain the purpose of assurance, what it covers, how it is prioritised and the strategic aims it serves for the sponsor and board.
question: A council's board is about to approve the construction contract for a new leisure centre. It commissions an independent review first. What is the purpose of that assurance, what should it look at, where should it focus, and why should it not simply be done by the project team itself?

teach.h: Assurance: can we trust what we're told?
teach.body: Assurance is the process of providing confidence to stakeholders, especially the governance board and sponsor, that the project will achieve its objectives: that it is on track and being managed properly. To be credible it should be independent of the team delivering the work. Plain English: the board cannot check everything itself, so assurance is a trusted second pair of eyes that says whether the reports, plans and business case can be relied on.

head: Area
The assurance question
rows: Are roles, authority and controls working?
Is the plan realistic and being followed?
Are risks known, owned and managed?
Will the outputs be fit for purpose?
Are the benefits still realistic and owned?
Are policies and regulations being met?

teach.h: Priorities: focus where risk and value are greatest
teach.caption: Assurance effort is limited, so it is prioritised towards the areas where failure would cost the most.

teach.body: Assurance serves three strategic aims. PROTECT THE INVESTMENT: spot problems early, before money is wasted, and stop projects that can no longer succeed. SUPPORT DECISIONS AT GATES: give the sponsor and board evidence-based confidence when deciding go, no-go or replan. IMPROVE DELIVERY: recommendations and shared lessons raise the standard of this project and future ones. Independence is what makes all three credible: a team marking its own homework cannot give the board real confidence.

teach.caption: Each line adds independence. The board gets most confidence from the lines furthest from delivery.

teach.body: Before the gate that releases the £12m construction contract, the board commissions a gateway review by people outside the project. Reviewers find the business case is two years old, energy costs have risen sharply, and three major risks have no owner. They report to the sponsor and board, not to the project manager alone. The board delays the gate by a month while the case is refreshed and risk owners are named, then approves with confidence.

In a LINEAR life cycle, assurance is usually aligned to decision gates: a gateway review before each go/no-go decision, plus periodic health checks or audits. In an ITERATIVE life cycle, assurance tends to be lighter and more frequent, timed around releases, and can use working product demonstrations, backlog health and release reviews as evidence. In both, the purpose is the same: independent confidence for the people directing the project.

teach.text: Classic confusions: assurance is NOT quality control (checking outputs) and NOT the project manager checking their own work. It gives the board and sponsor independent confidence about the whole project. An audit is one FORM of assurance, not a synonym for it.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Purpose: independent confidence for the board and sponsor that objectives will be met.
Scope: governance, plans, business case, risk, quality, benefits, compliance.
Priorities: focus effort on the areas of greatest risk and value.
Strategic aims: protect investment, support gate decisions, improve delivery.
Explain why independence matters, and name a form (audit, gateway review, peer review).
Assurance gives stakeholders, especially the board, confidence the project will succeed.
It should be independent of the delivery team.
Scope: governance, plans, business case, risk, quality, benefits, compliance.
Priorities: greatest risk and value first.
Aims: protect investment, support gate decisions, improve delivery.

summary: You can now explain the purpose of assurance and why it must be independent, describe its scope, and explain how it is prioritised. You can also state its strategic aims and recognise its common forms and the three lines of assurance.

A.q: What is the MAIN purpose of assurance on a project?
options: To check each output against its spec
To replace the project manager's reports
To give confidence it will succeed
To set the tolerances for the project
A.why: Assurance provides confidence to stakeholders, especially the board and sponsor, that the project will achieve its objectives.

whyNot.0: Checking outputs against a specification is quality control.
whyNot.1: Assurance tests the reliability of reports; it does not replace them.
whyNot.3: Tolerances are delegated by the sponsor and board.

A.q: Why should assurance be independent of the delivery team?
options: So the team can skip reporting
So the PM can approve the gates
So the PMO owns the business case
A.why: Independence means reviewers have no stake in the result, so the board can trust their findings.

whyNot.1: The team still reports; assurance tests whether those reports can be relied on.
whyNot.2: Gate decisions belong to the sponsor and board.
whyNot.3: The sponsor owns the business case.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT within the typical scope of project assurance?
options: Whether the business case still holds
Whether risks are owned and managed
Which daily tasks the team picks up
A.why: Assurance looks at governance, plans, business case, risk, quality, benefits and compliance. Daily task allocation is the PM's management, not assurance scope.

whyNot.0: The business case is a core assurance area.
whyNot.1: Risk management is a core assurance area.
whyNot.2: Compliance is a core assurance area.

B.q: An assurance team has time for only one in-depth review this quarter. Which project should it prioritise?
options: A high-value, high-risk core IT change
B.why: Assurance is prioritised towards the areas of greatest risk and value, where failure would cost the most.

whyNot.0: Low value and low risk needs only a light touch.
whyNot.2: This may merit a targeted review, but it carries less at stake than a high-value, high-risk project.
whyNot.3: High value but low risk needs regular checks, not the deepest review.

B.q: Which of the following is a STRATEGIC AIM of assurance?
B.why: Assurance aims to protect the investment, support decisions at gates and improve delivery.

whyNot.0: Managing workload is the project manager's job.
whyNot.1: Writing the PMP is the project manager's job.
whyNot.2: Prioritising the backlog is the product owner's job.

B.q: In the 'three lines' model, which line gives the board the MOST independent assurance?
B.why: The third line, independent internal or external audit, is furthest from delivery and therefore the most independent.

whyNot.1: Self-checks are the first line: closest to the work, least independent.
whyNot.2: PMO health checks are second line: useful, but inside the organisation's own functions.
whyNot.3: A status report is the PM's management information, not independent assurance.

C.q: A gateway review before the main build contract finds the business case is out of date and the benefits have not been re-checked. How should these findings BEST be used?
options: Sent only to the project team to fix
Used by the board at the gate
Used to replace the project manager
C.why: Assurance exists to support decisions at gates: the board uses the findings to decide go, no-go or replan, and to require the business case to be refreshed.

whyNot.0: Waiting until the end throws away the chance to act before committing money.
whyNot.1: The team must act, but the findings' main audience is the board making the decision.
whyNot.3: Assurance is about confidence and improvement, not automatically replacing people.

C.q: An organisation adopts an iterative life cycle for its digital projects. How is assurance MOST likely to adapt?
options: It happens only once, at final release
The product owner becomes the auditor
C.why: Iterative assurance is usually lighter and more frequent, aligned to releases, using demos and release reviews as evidence. It remains independent.

whyNot.0: Iterative projects still need independent assurance for the board.
whyNot.2: One review at the end would be far too late to support decisions.
whyNot.3: The product owner is part of delivery, so cannot provide independent assurance.

C.q: To save money, a project manager proposes that his own team provides all assurance to the board. What is the BEST assessment?
options: Sound, as the team knows the most
Sound, if the PMO is kept informed
Weak, as it costs more than an audit
C.why: Assurance must be independent of the delivery team to give the board credible confidence. Self-assurance is only the first line.

whyNot.0: Knowledge is not the issue; a team cannot objectively assure its own work.
whyNot.1: Informing the PMO does not make the assurance independent.
whyNot.2: The problem is independence, not cost; self-checking is usually cheaper.

reteach.title: Buying a house with a survey
reteach.question: You are about to buy a house. The seller says it is in perfect condition. Why do you pay for an independent survey, and what should it look at?

blocks.body: You are the board: about to commit a large sum. The seller is the delivery team: they may be honest, but they are not independent. The surveyor gives you confidence by checking what matters most (roof, structure, damp), not every light switch. Their report helps you decide: buy, renegotiate, or walk away. That is protecting the investment, supporting the decision and, through the recommendations, improving what happens next.

blocks.text: Asking the seller to do the survey would be cheaper, but you would not trust it. That is why assurance must be independent of the people delivering the work.

explain.body: Assurance provides confidence to stakeholders, especially the board and sponsor, that the project will achieve its objectives. It should be independent of the delivery team so its findings can be trusted.

test.q: Who is project assurance MAINLY intended to give confidence to?
test.why: Assurance gives the governance board and sponsor confidence that the project is on track and well managed.

whyNot.0: Suppliers are delivery partners, not the main audience for assurance.
whyNot.1: The team is what is being assured; it is not the main audience.
whyNot.3: Customers benefit indirectly, but assurance reports go to the board and sponsor.

explain.body: Assurance can cover governance, plans, the business case, risk, quality, benefits and compliance. A review might cover all of them or focus on a few.

test.q: An assurance reviewer checks that a project's handling of customer data meets UK GDPR. Which area of scope is this?
test.why: Checking that the project meets legal and regulatory duties is compliance assurance.

whyNot.0: Benefits assurance asks whether the benefits are still realistic and owned.
whyNot.2: Governance assurance checks roles, authority and controls; a legal duty check is compliance.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance asks whether outputs will be fit for purpose.

explain.body: Assurance effort is limited, so it targets the areas of greatest risk and value. Its strategic aims: protect the investment, support decisions at gates and improve delivery.

test.q: Why is assurance focused on the areas of greatest risk and value?
options: Effort goes where failure costs most
Auditors can only review one project
High-value work needs no business case
test.why: Assurance resources are limited, so they are directed to where problems would do the most damage.

whyNot.1: Low-risk work is still governed, just with lighter assurance.
whyNot.2: There is no rule limiting auditors to one project.
whyNot.3: High-value work needs a strong business case more than ever.

explain.body: Forms include audits, gateway and health-check reviews, and peer reviews. The three lines: the project team (first), organisational functions such as the PMO (second), and independent internal or external audit (third).

test.q: A health check carried out by the organisation's central PMO belongs to which line of assurance?
test.why: Organisational functions such as the PMO provide second-line assurance: more independent than the team, less than audit.

whyNot.0: The first line is the project team checking itself.
whyNot.1: The third line is independent internal or external audit.
whyNot.2: PMO health checks are a recognised form of assurance.
